questions.question: What must an identity element do to every element of the set?
options: Make the operation commutative.
Send it to zero.
Swap it with its inverse.
Leave it unchanged on both sides.

questions.question: Why is “on both sides” included for an identity element?
options: Because the identity must be outside the set.
A one-sided neutral element may not be neutral when placed on the other side.
Because every operation is commutative.
Because binary operations always have two different identities.

questions.question: If an identity element exists for a binary operation, how many can there be?
options: Infinitely many whenever the set is nonempty.
At most one.
Exactly two.
One for each element of the set.

questions.question: Why is the identity element operation-dependent?
options: An identity element is chosen only by notation.
The same set cannot carry two operations.
Every operation has identity $0$.
$0$ for addition, $1$ for multiplication.

questions.question: What is the difference between an identity element and an absorbing element?
options: Identity leaves elements unchanged; absorbing collapses them.
An absorbing element must be outside the set.
An identity changes every element into its inverse.
They are the same concept in every operation.

questions.question: What is the identity element of $(\mathbb R,+)$?
options: There is no identity element.

questions.question: What is the identity element of $(\mathbb R,\cdot)$?
options: Every real number.

questions.question: For $a\star b=a+b+1$ on $\mathbb R$, what is the identity element?
options: No identity exists.

questions.question: For $2\times2$ matrices under multiplication, what is the identity element?
options: Any diagonal matrix.
The matrix with all entries equal to $1$.
The zero $2\times2$ matrix.

questions.question: For the operation $a\star b=\max(a,b)$ on $\{0,1,2\}$, what is the identity element?
options: No identity exists.

questions.question: Why does the uniqueness proof for identity elements start by comparing two candidates $e$ and $f$?
options: Because identities are never comparable.
Because associativity is needed to subtract them.
Because one identity must be left-sided and the other right-sided.
Because $e\star f$ must equal both $f$ and $e$.

questions.question: Does the existence of an identity element imply that every element has an inverse?
options: No, because identities are not allowed in monoids.
Yes, but only for finite sets.
Yes. The inverse of every element is the identity.
No; a monoid may have an identity without inverses.

questions.question: If $e$ satisfies only $a\star e=a$ for all $a$, what is still missing for $e$ to be an identity element?
options: Associativity of $e$ alone.
The condition $a\star e=e$ for all $a$.
Commutativity of every operation on every set.
The condition $e\star a=a$ for all $a$.

questions.question: For $a\star b=a+b-5$ on $\mathbb R$, what is the identity element?
options: No identity exists.

questions.question: For $a\star b=ab+a+b$ on $\mathbb R$, what is the identity element?
options: No identity exists.

questions.question: On the positive real numbers under addition, why is there no identity element?
options: Addition is not closed on positive real numbers.
The additive identity would be $0$, but $0$ is not positive.
The identity would be $1$, but $1$ is positive.
Every positive number is an identity.

questions.question: Why can changing the underlying set destroy an identity element even when the formula for the operation is unchanged?
options: The operation automatically becomes non-associative.
The neutral element might no longer belong to the set.
The neutral element is allowed to lie outside the set.
The operation automatically becomes commutative.

questions.question: For a noncommutative operation, why is a right identity not enough?
options: A right identity is never an element of the set.
It may fail to leave elements unchanged when placed on the left.
A right identity makes the operation undefined.
A right identity always implies all inverses exist.

questions.question: On a set $A$ with more than one element, define $a\star b=a$. Does this operation have a two-sided identity?
options: No, because the rule is not a binary operation.
Yes. The first element of $A$ is the identity.
Yes. Every element is a two-sided identity.
No; all are right identities, but none works on the left.

questions.question: For $a\star b=(a+b)/2$ on $\mathbb R$, why is there no identity element?
options: Solving $(a+e)/2=a$ gives $e=a$, which cannot be one fixed element for all $a$.
The operation is not closed on $\mathbb R$.
The identity is $1$ because averages with one change nothing.
The identity is $0$ because averages with zero change nothing.
